analysis.title: EM Macro Themes: Oil's Shocking Effects on Growth, Inflation and BoPs
key_insights: Eight months into the Iran conflict, the oil shock has had a muted effect on EM growth and inflation. High-frequency activity data show EM growth stable at an above-trend rate. DM growth has accelerated to its fastest pace since the post-pandemic recovery.
Inflation has risen by less than expected in both EMs and DMs. Early concerns about a 2021/22-style inflation shock now look unlikely.

The muted response partly reflects one-off offsets: government subsidies, taxes and fuel-market regulation (especially in Asian EMs), the AI investment boom, unusually weak food inflation, strong EM FX and negative output gaps.

Structural factors also limit the shock. In real terms the oil price rise is moderate by historical standards, even with wider diesel and gasoline spreads, and the fossil-fuel energy needed per unit of real output has fallen steadily in both EMs and DMs.
GS estimates that a 10% rise in oil prices lowers GDP in oil-importing economies by 0.2-0.3pp over 1-2 years on average. The loss rises to 0.5-0.6pp for supply-driven shocks.

GS estimates that a 10% rise in oil prices raises the level of CPI by 0.3pp on average over one year, with country estimates ranging from 0.1pp to 0.7pp. Oil exporters and administered-price markets sit at the low end, and faster pass-through EMs in Asia and LatAm at the high end.

Current account effects track net oil exports as a share of GDP and emerge mostly within 1-2 quarters, because long-term oil contracts fix volumes but not prices. The exception is oil-indexed LNG contracts (Qatar, Algeria, Nigeria), which can lag pricing by three to six months.

Growth estimates are highly sensitive to whether the shock is demand- or supply-driven, to the sample period and to the specification. GS therefore blends empirical SVAR estimates with calibrations based on net fuel exports, weighting the calibration 70% for GDP and 50% for the current account.

This year's shock is supply-driven because Gulf supply was reduced. Most empirical identification strategies would label it demand-driven because global growth was accelerating before and after its onset, so misidentification can bias the estimates.

EM Asia is the most exposed region. It dominates the negative end of the GDP and current account distributions, and several of its economies have high CPI responses. DMs and LatAm cluster near -0.3pp on GDP, with Chile showing the largest CPI response in the sample.
CEEMEA has the most polarized effects. The Gulf exporters and Kazakhstan benefit most, while Lebanon, Ukraine and Kenya are among the hardest hit.
Blended current account responses to a 10% oil shock range from -1.2pp of GDP in Lebanon to +3.5pp in Kuwait.
GS warns against complacency. Oil prices could rise further and, on its estimates, still generate significant economic shocks.

Appendix I gives a country-by-country guide to fuel market structure, CPI fuel weights, net fuel exports and the extraordinary measures introduced since the conflict began, including fuel tax cuts, price caps and targeted subsidies. The regulation index was built by an AI agent from the World Bank fuel subsidy database and validated by GS country economists.

macro_indicators.indicator: Real GDP response to a 10% oil price rise, oil importers
macro_indicators.reading: -0.2 to -0.3pp on average over 1-2 years, -0.5 to -0.6pp for supply shocks
macro_indicators.interpretation: Oil importers lose modest output from an oil price rise, with supply-driven shocks costing roughly twice as much because they lack the offsetting global demand.

macro_indicators.indicator: CPI response to a 10% oil price rise
macro_indicators.reading: +0.3pp on average over one year, range 0.1pp to 0.7pp
macro_indicators.interpretation: Pass-through to headline inflation is modest on average and highest in EMs with fast pass-through and weaker nominal anchors.

macro_indicators.indicator: Median oil importer real GDP response, supply shock
macro_indicators.interpretation: A supply-driven oil shock is a terms-of-trade loss for importers, so growth falls well below the average estimate.

macro_indicators.indicator: Median oil importer real GDP response, demand shock
macro_indicators.interpretation: A demand-driven oil rise coincides with stronger global activity, which more than offsets the terms-of-trade loss.

macro_indicators.indicator: Blended current account response to a 10% oil shock
macro_indicators.interpretation: Current account swings follow net oil export positions, with Gulf exporters gaining and Lebanon, Thailand, Ukraine, Chile and Pakistan losing most.

risk_factors: Oil prices could rise further and generate significant economic shocks, especially if the shock is supply-driven.
The one-off offsets (government fuel-price intervention, strong EM FX, the AI boom and weak food inflation) may not persist.
El Niño risks and rising fertilizer prices could end the unusually weak food inflation that has offset energy inflation.
Empirical GDP estimates are sensitive to shock identification, sample period and specification, so the true growth hit could differ from the estimates.
Fuel subsidy and price control programs create fiscal strain and smuggling or diversion problems in several markets.
charts_described: Exhibit 2 plots nominal and real Brent (2025 US$) against a 50-year real average of US$79/bbl, showing the current real price about 25% above that average and moderate versus past crises.
Exhibit 10 plots GDP, current account and CPI responses to an oil shock against net fuel exports and CPI weights, with R² of 0.14, 0.84 and 0.00 respectively.
Exhibit 9 shows impulse responses for oil importers to a 10% oil shock, with GDP falling under supply shocks and rising under demand shocks.
geopolitical: Iran conflict, now in its eighth month, has reduced oil supply from the Gulf and pushed oil prices sharply higher.
Governments across Asian EMs, CEEMEA, LatAm and DMs have introduced fuel subsidies, tax cuts, price caps and margin caps in response to the conflict.
The US released barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and relaxed Jones Act shipping rules to ease oil supply and prices.

tension_points.bull_case: EM growth has held at an above-trend pace and inflation has risen less than feared. Government intervention, strong EM FX, the AI boom and weak food inflation offset the shock, and oil intensity of production has fallen.
tension_points.bear_case: The offsets are partly one-off and oil prices could rise further. A supply-driven shock costs importers 0.5-0.6pp of GDP per 10% rise versus 0.2-0.3pp on average, and empirical methods may misclassify this year's supply shock as demand-driven.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Further oil price rises, or the one-off offsets (fuel-price intervention, strong EM FX, the AI boom, weak food inflation) fading, would invalidate the muted-impact view.

theme_stances.key_argument: EM growth and inflation have barely reacted to the oil shock because of one-off offsets and a moderate real price rise.
theme_stances.evidence: 2021/22-style inflation shock now appearing well wide of the mark

theme_stances.key_argument: EM Asia dominates the negative end of the GDP and current account distributions and has several high CPI responses.
theme_stances.evidence: EM Asia is the most exposed
